extracted.intended_audience: novelists, fiction writers, and critics studying craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and managing a novelist's methods—scenic vs panoramic presentation, centre of vision (point of view), the role of scene and summary, and how to blend or restrict techniques to suit a subject. Focused on constructing coherent narrative treatment across a novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish scenic and panoramic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether an episode is to be presented as a single, particular hour (scenic) or as a broad, general survey (panoramic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the scenic when you want immediate, concentrated depiction of emotion and incident; use the panoramic to give a wide, survey-like impression of a social landscape. A novelist may legitimately alternate the two methods, even on the same page, to suit the exigencies of the story (examples: Flaubert’s ball = pictorial/single hour; Thackeray’s Vanity Fair = panoramic sweep).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial vs dramatic treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether a passage is to be 'pictorial' (bathed in the climate of a character’s mood, subjective rendering) or 'dramatic' (objective, as it would appear staged).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pictorial passages center on a character’s inner perception and feeling; dramatic passages place visible and audible facts to the fore and could be acted on stage without losing the main impression (examples: Madame Bovary’s ball = pictorial; the cattle-show/comices = dramatic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure scenes are necessary and prepared
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene must be placed where everything is ready for it, where it will thoroughly illuminate a new face of the subject and advance the action by a definite stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid scenes that do nothing in particular; a 'scene that is not really wanted' or that 'for lack of preparation fails to make its effect' is a weakness. Plan summaries and chronicle passages to prepare and lead into scenes so the scene's opportunity is ripe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene as primary means to start interest and climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Use scenes to begin interest (drop into a scene on the first page) and to perform climactic work (a scene completes what it began).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a scene is the readiest means of raising a question and later providing resolution, distribute scenes to articulate the book's structure and to provide recurring focal points for climax and resolution (examples: the ball, the comices, the theatre evening, the interview in the cathedral, the deathbed session in Madame Bovary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent on some plan; limit latitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever methods are used, follow the principle adopted and allow no more latitude than required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A novelist should retain liberty to draw on resources (drama, pictorial description) as needed, but must avoid random or ungoverned mixture. Critics look for the organizing principle that governs how methods are mingled and varied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriate centre of vision (point of view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide with which character (if any) the writer identifies and from whose mind the subject is primarily revealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject can be rendered by a single figure’s perception, persist with that centre; unnecessary plunges into other minds confuse. But if part of the subject must be seen from without, the author must shift viewpoint judiciously and prepare for those shifts (example: Madame Bovary mainly through Emma’s eyes, but occasional other centres are used for necessity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid haphazard plunges into characters' inner lives
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not shift into interior consciousness without compensating gain; random changes of focus only confuse the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift viewpoint only when the subject requires it, and minimize frequency so that the reader's sense of narrative focus is not disrupted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply perspectives the principal character cannot provide
rubrics_metrics.description: If the main character’s intelligence or perception is insufficient to reveal essential aspects of the world, the author must supply another vision (often his own) to fill the gap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the protagonist is a 'simple soul' or dull intelligence, the narrative must move beyond that consciousness to render setting, irony, or social reality (example: Emma cannot fully reveal Yonville; the author's mind must intervene).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make viewpoint transitions without awkwardness or self-exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: When shifting from a character’s consciousness to the author's own standpoint, the transition should be disguised and softened to avoid jolting the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid openly 'going behind' the character or plainly asserting the author’s freedom to comment; the novelist should effect transitions subtly so shared immersion in a character's experience is not rendered unreal by abrupt authorial intrusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an authorial tone that allows ironic distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a controlled irony or aloofness so that readers are not wholly identified with a character’s limited vision, allowing the author to step in when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flaubert’s technique: make the character subjective but with an 'air of aloofness' so a hint of irony prevents total immersion; irony permits the author to supersede the character’s view without dislocating the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat setting and secondary figures as integral, not mere background
rubrics_metrics.description: Render the protagonist’s world—town, types, neighbours—with as much distinctness and characterization as the main figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The environment should belong to the treatment integrally; it should not be a softened background but appear fully to the front, so that the interplay between character and environment is visible (example: Yonville is as intensively treated as Emma).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame narrative elements to serve overarching structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange early episodes and auxiliary characters so they serve later structural needs (e.g., prepare a secondary character whose perspective is required for the climax).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce and develop other characters’ histories in advance if they are needed later (example: Charles’s early history prepares the final discovery and frames Emma’s story so the book 'opens and closes' within his affair as well).

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the subject determine the method
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose method because the subject calls for it; the nature of the theme will often pull toward scenic or panoramic, pictorial or dramatic treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A writer’s subject is the chief guide: if the subject asks for a single unmixed manner, adopt it; otherwise, select and vary methods that best reveal the latent idea in the material (examples: where Emma’s case favors pictorial treatment, Thackeray’s subjects favor panorama).

rubrics_metrics.name: Layer and stratify methods thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange methods so they may be alternated, united, or blended—creating 'layers and stratifications' in narrative treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In well-fashioned work it is interesting to discover how method is laid upon method; combine dramatic action with pictorial rendering, blend points of view, and use these stratifications to enrich the reader's understanding rather than to confuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use economy: 'no more latitude than he requires'
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow the novelist only as much freedom of method as the subject and effect demand; avoid unnecessary indulgence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first of an artist’s precepts is to allow himself no more latitude than required; precision and restraint in method preserve unity and effect.
